item.title: Anthropic Filed an S-1. ANT Is No Small Bug.
item.dc:creator: He Ren
item.description:
Back in May, I wrote about SpaceX’s S-1, the one that read like a magazine. Buried in it was a contract that made me re-read the page twice: Anthropic had agreed to pay SpaceX $1.25 billion a month for GPUs. I called it buying batteries from your ex.

Five months later, the customer has filed its own S-1. And the ex is now sending a bigger bill.

Anthropic’s registration statement went to the SEC on October 26, 2026. It is about 335 pages before the financial statements, and it is less of a coffee-table magazine than SpaceX’s. There are eight glossy full-page graphics up front and a stack of customer case studies, but nothing is on fire. What it has instead is numbers. Very large numbers, some of them with a minus sign, and a corporate governance section that reads like the rules of a board game invented by philosophers.

Let’s walk through it.

What Was Filed

The company is Anthropic, PBC, a Delaware public benefit corporation based in San Francisco. The ticker will be ANT, on the Nasdaq Global Select Market.

Yes, ANT. A company whose entire pitch is building something enormous chose the name of the smallest thing at the picnic. I respect it. Ants are also famous for carrying many times their body weight, which, as we’ll see in the compute section, is the right metaphor.

Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley lead the deal, the same two banks that ran SpaceX. Behind them come twenty more banks, from J.P. Morgan and Citigroup down to Macquarie and Capital One. Twenty-two underwriters in total. SpaceX had twenty-three. I assume there is a group chat.

What the filing does not have yet: the price range, the number of shares, the deal size, the run-rate revenue figure, and the third-quarter income statement. All of those are literally blank in this preliminary version (a row of “$” signs with nothing after them). Companies fill them in closer to the roadshow. So anything you read about the valuation right now is either an estimate or a guess, including mine below.

The Income Statement: Fourteen Times in One Year

Here is the top line, straight from the summary financial data (p. 22):

USD millions. Source: Form S-1, Summary Consolidated Financial and Other Data, p. 22.
2023 2024 2025 H1 2025 H1 2026
Revenue 41 386 4,585 1,163 16,286
Compute and infrastructure 433 2,522 7,326 2,334 8,945
Personnel 95 454 1,839 538 3,152
Sales, marketing, and partnerships 2 43 568 120 3,168
Other operating and administrative 62 347 1,412 306 1,714
Bartz settlement 1,500
Operating loss (551) (2,980) (8,060) (2,135) (693)
Net loss (1,531) (8,309) (41,965) (12,969) (80,748)

Read the first row again. Revenue in the first half of 2026 was $16.3 billion, which is 14 times the first half of 2025 and more than three and a half times all of 2025. The company went from $41 million of revenue in 2023 to more than $11.5 billion in a single quarter. If a student handed me this in a valuation case, I would ask them to check their units.

The quarterly view (p. 157) is where the story gets interesting:

For every quarter of 2025, the compute bill was bigger than revenue. In Q1 2026 revenue finally passed it, and in Q2 2026 revenue ($11.6 billion) was more than double compute ($5.6 billion). That quarter produced Anthropic’s first operating profit: $974 million (p. 157).

A few other things worth noticing in that table:

  • The Bartz line. That $1.5 billion in 2025 is the settlement of the authors’ copyright class action, booked in Q3 2025 (pp. 22, 157). In that quarter it equaled about 109% of revenue. It is the most expensive library card in history.
  • Sales, marketing, and partnerships jumped 26-fold in the first half of 2026. That line is mostly fees paid to channel partners, meaning the cloud platforms that resell Claude (p. 146). The S-1 says the increase was “primarily driven by a $2.7 billion increase in fees paid to channel partners” (p. 149). Translation: Amazon, Google, and Microsoft take a toll on the highway.
  • Revenue is booked gross. When a customer buys through a cloud marketplace, Anthropic records the full amount as revenue and the platform’s cut as an expense (F-21). Worth remembering before comparing margins to companies that net it out.

The $80.7 Billion Loss That Mostly Isn’t

Now the scary number. Net loss for the first half of 2026 was $80.7 billion, on $16.3 billion of revenue. That is a net margin of roughly negative 496%, and it is the figure most headlines led with.

It is also mostly accounting.

Anthropic financed itself partly with convertible notes sold to strategic partners, especially Amazon, and with other note purchase agreements. Those instruments are carried at fair value. When the company’s valuation goes up, the notes (which will convert into shares) become more valuable, and the company has to record the increase as a loss. The S-1 says the $72.4 billion change was “primarily driven by an increase in the fair value of our outstanding convertible promissory notes resulting from an increase in our enterprise valuation” (p. 22). The extra $8.8 billion of “other expense” comes from the fair value of assets and liabilities under the same note purchase agreements (p. 150).

So here is a company that loses more money the more successful it becomes. In finance class we call this a non-cash, non-operating item. In real life it is a strange kind of humblebrag.

The operating business tells a calmer story: an operating loss of only $693 million for the half, and positive operating cash flow of $3.9 billion (p. 168), against cash burned in every prior year. Management’s own non-GAAP measure, adjusted operating income, was +$1.6 billion for the half, a 10% margin (p. 156). The usual caveat applies: non-GAAP adds back stock-based compensation, which was $2.2 billion for the half and is about to get much larger (more on that below).

The Cost of Compute: Every Chip, From Everyone

If there is one thing to understand about a frontier AI lab, it is that the product is made of electricity and silicon. Anthropic’s largest expense line is literally called “Compute and infrastructure,” and the trend in that line is the single best chart in the filing:

The S-1 puts it this way: revenue “grew 1,368% year over year for the three months ended June 30, 2026 compared to compute and infrastructure expenses that grew 300%” (p. 10). That gap is the whole investment case in one sentence.

There is also a hidden gross margin. The face of the income statement shows expenses by nature (compute, people, and so on), not by function, so there is no “gross profit” line. But Note 8 to the financial statements reports a functional split, with a cost of revenue of $2,380 million for the first half of 2026 (F-39). My own arithmetic from that note:

USD millions. Revenue and cost of revenue from Form S-1, Note 8 (F-39); gross margin is the author’s calculation and is not reported in the filing.
2023 2024 2025 H1 2025 H1 2026
Revenue 41 386 4,585 1,163 16,286
Cost of revenue 26 752 2,773 1,019 2,380
Implied gross margin 37% (95%) 40% 12% 85%

An 85% gross margin is software-like. The catch is that serving customers (inference) is cheap relative to building the next model (training and research), which sits in R&D. R&D was $9.7 billion in the same half (F-39). The product is profitable to sell; it is expensive to keep improving.

Who supplies the compute

Anthropic says it trains and serves its models on “four major chip families (AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs)” (p. 135). That is unusual. Most labs pick a side. Anthropic picked all of them, and the contracts in the MD&A (pp. 170 to 172) show what that costs:

Some details that do not fit on a bar:

  • SpaceXAI (formerly X.AI, now a SpaceX subsidiary): up to $120.5 billion for NVIDIA GPUs, terms into 2029, “approximately $3.1 billion in the aggregate per month once all capacity has been delivered, which we expect in December 2026” (p. 171). In May the bill was $1.25 billion a month. Now it is $3.1 billion. The ex has upgraded you to the premium plan. To be fair to Anthropic, after the initial periods end in early 2027, either side can cancel with 90 days’ notice.
  • Google: at least $114.5 billion through July 2033, “regardless of actual usage,” plus an estimated $125 to $150 billion of additional TPU compute for 2028 to 2031 that is not in the commitments table (p. 170).
  • Amazon: at least $110.0 billion from May 2026 to April 2036, also regardless of actual usage (p. 171).
  • Microsoft: at least $44.9 billion from November 2026 to May 2033 (p. 170).
  • Broadcom: five-year leases on TPU equipment with total rent of about $161.2 billion (p. 171).
  • Plus Nscale ($44.6 billion), Lambda ($41.3 billion), and AMD (more than $20 billion for the first tranche of its new rack systems).

The notes to the financial statements give the totals: fixed or minimum commitments of about $265.6 billion as of June 30, 2026 (F-58), and about $245 billion more signed after that date (F-65). Half a trillion dollars, give or take, before counting the open-ended deals.

For perspective, Anthropic’s revenue in the first half of 2026 was $16.3 billion. These are bets that revenue keeps compounding for a decade. Most of these contracts are non-cancelable. If demand slows, the bill does not.

One more twist: the compute suppliers are also the financiers. Amazon holds $6.2 billion of convertible notes. Google has a $20 billion note facility and an option to buy up to $10 billion of stock alongside the IPO. Broadcom has a $42 billion facility that can only be used to pay Broadcom’s own lease rent, at a 9% paid-in-kind interest rate (p. 165). AMD committed to buy up to $5 billion of stock as its chips get delivered (p. 163). The landlord lends you the money to pay the landlord. Vendor financing has a long and colorful history in tech; this is the largest version I have seen.

Who the Customers Are

Anthropic is primarily an enterprise business. As of September 30, 2026 (pp. 9, 142):

  • More than 11,900 customers spent $100,000 or more over the trailing twelve months.
  • More than 1,900 spent $1 million or more.
  • About 250 spent $10 million or more.
  • About 40 million customers spent less than $100,000 each.

The $100K club includes “every company in the Fortune 10, over 50% of the Fortune 500, and over 30% of the Global 2000” (p. 194). Yet for the average Fortune 500 customer, Anthropic’s revenue is “less than 0.1% of their total expenses” (p. 142). That is the “we have barely started” slide every IPO wants, and here it comes with a footnote.

How much do the biggest customers matter? Less than you might fear, more than you might like:

Author’s summary of customer and channel disclosures in Form S-1.
Concentration measure Figure Source
Any single customer above 10% of revenue, 9M 2026 None p. 56
Top five customers, share of revenue, 9M 2026 About 25% p. 56
Revenue sold through cloud marketplaces (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure), H1 2026 48% p. 56
Same, 2023 11% p. 56
Revenue from consumption (usage) vs. subscriptions, H1 2026 80% / 20% p. 138
U.S. share of revenue, H1 2026 72% F-26

The real concentration is not a customer; it is a channel. Nearly half of revenue now flows through the same three cloud companies that sell Anthropic its compute, own pieces of its equity, and, as the risk factors note, compete with it (p. 73). It is a very tight family.

Two smaller disclosures made me smile:

  • Net Revenue Retention of about 900% as of September 30, 2026 (p. 135). For context, a SaaS company bragging about 130% gets a standing ovation. Nine hundred percent means the average qualifying customer spends nine times what it spent a year earlier.
  • Holiday code freezes cost real money. In the two weeks ended January 2, 2026, total customer spend fell about 20% compared to the prior two weeks, because engineers stopped shipping code for the holidays (p. 143). Even the AI takes Christmas off when its users do.

And one that made me appreciate the honesty: the company estimates that 5% to 7% of revenue in the first nine months of 2026 came from customers who were later found to be violating its usage policy or commercial terms (p. 145). It expects that share to decline as enforcement improves. I can’t remember the last S-1 that quantified its bad customers.

Growth Outlook: How Long Can This Last?

The S-1 is careful not to forecast, so here is what it does give us:

  • Remaining performance obligations of $10.8 billion at June 30, 2026, about 75% expected within twelve months (F-26).
  • Revenue per employee of more than $6.6 million on a trailing basis, up from $1.4 million a year earlier, with about 5,300 employees (pp. 10, 229).
  • Cash and cash equivalents of $112.4 billion plus $19.3 billion of short-term investments at June 30, 2026, after raising $141.1 billion of capital in total (p. 10). Add $77 billion of undrawn note facilities and a $15 billion credit line (pp. 162, 165).
  • A self-described market opportunity of “more than $40 trillion” of knowledge work globally (p. 185), which is the kind of number you put in an S-1 when “very big” won’t fit in the table.

The line that best captures the growth thesis is this one: “over 90% of the contributions to our codebase in September 2026 were written by Claude” (p. 136). The product is building the product. Whether that is a flywheel or a hall of mirrors is the question a public investor is being asked to price.

Ownership: Five Classes of Stock, Two Single Shares

The SpaceX S-1 had a simple control story: Musk’s Class B gets ten votes per share. Anthropic’s version needs a table.

Author’s summary from the Form S-1 cover page and “Our Governance Structure and Its Goals,” pp. 242 to 253.
Class Who holds it Votes Economics
A Public investors, founders, employees 1 per share Yes
N “Primarily strategic business partners” (Amazon, Google, and others) None Yes, same as A
T One share, held by the Long-Term Benefit Trust Elects a majority of the board None
F One share, held by an LLC of the seven co-founders Fixed 50.1% of total voting power None
E Employees (not founders), earned by tenure Limited matters only None

Let that sink in. One share (Class T) lets the Long-Term Benefit Trust elect a majority of the board. One other share (Class F) gives the co-founders 50.1% of all stockholder votes, and that percentage does not dilute no matter how many new shares are issued (p. 117). The S-1 is admirably blunt about what this means for you, the Class A buyer:

holders of our Class A common stock generally will not be able to affect the outcome of any matter submitted to a vote of our stockholders or the election of our directors, regardless of how they vote

Form S-1, Risk Factors, p. 108

Some features worth knowing:

  • The Trust. The Long-Term Benefit Trust is meant to be five “financially disinterested” trustees with expertise in AI safety, national security, and public policy (p. 13). Four seats are filled today, and one of the trustees is Ben Bernanke (p. 245). The former Fed Chair now helps oversee an AI lab. Trustees are paid $400,000 a year in cash and are prohibited from owning the stock (pp. 108, 246).
  • The founders. The 50.1% voting share sunsets only when fewer than three of the seven co-founders remain active for 90 consecutive days, followed by a 450-day transition period (pp. 108, 247). There is no fixed calendar date.
  • The strategic investors have no vote. Amazon and Google hold non-voting Class N stock, so they don’t appear in the principal stockholders table at all. Google’s stake is capped at 14.99% and Amazon’s at 12% under their financing agreements (pp. 164, 168).
  • Index risk. The S-1 itself warns that its “multi-class capital structure may make us ineligible for inclusion in indices,” so passive funds might not buy it (p. 109). Same issue SpaceX flagged.
  • Philanthropy, built into the cap table. Anthropic contributed 846,840,960 Class N shares, 5% of its fully diluted shares, to its own Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, and the board may add up to 2% more every time the stock price rises 50% (p. 12). The co-founders have each pledged 80% of their personal equity to philanthropy. Your dilution is someone’s endowment.

A napkin valuation

The filing does not state a valuation, so this part is mine, not the S-1’s. The most recent private round, Series H-1 in May and June 2026, priced at $589.0095 per preferred share, or about $58.90 per common share after the 10-for-1 stock split in September (pp. 282 to 283). The public benefit contribution implies about 16.9 billion fully diluted shares at June 30, 2026 (846.8 million is 5%, p. 12). Multiply, and the last private round valued Anthropic at roughly $1 trillion.

Against an annualized first-half revenue run of about $32.6 billion, that is around 30 times sales. The IPO price will tell us what public markets think. Remember that the price range is still blank.

Also on the “know before you buy” list: $26.6 billion of unrecognized stock compensation, much of which will hit the income statement when the IPO happens (p. 173). Expect the first public quarter to look ugly on a GAAP basis for that reason alone.

The Risk Factors Worth Reading

The risk factors run from page 26 to page 119. Most are standard. A handful are not:

  • The government fight. In February 2026, after the company said its technology should not be used for mass domestic surveillance or fully autonomous weapons, “the President of the United States stated that he had directed that all federal executive agencies cease using our technology” (p. 71). The Department of War labeled Anthropic a supply-chain risk. The company won in district court; an appeals court ruled 2 to 1 against it on one designation, and it has asked for rehearing (pp. 71 to 72, F-64). This is still live.
  • Export controls. In June 2026, the Commerce Department imposed worldwide restrictions on two of Anthropic’s most advanced models, and the company disabled them for all customers until the restrictions were lifted (p. 99). A product recall, but for intelligence.
  • The models themselves. The filing discloses that models, “including our own, have exhibited… unexpected strategic or self-preserving behaviors, including attempts to resist shutdown,” and even “behavior resembling blackmail” (p. 46). It also notes “we have observed models behaving differently when they detect or infer that they are being evaluated” (p. 46). I have read many S-1s. This is the first one where the product might be grading the auditor.
  • Copyright. Beyond the $1.5 billion Bartz settlement, music publishers, Reddit, and several Canadian news organizations have pending claims (pp. 240 to 241).
  • Concentrated suppliers. The company relies on “a limited number of CSPs” (Amazon, Google, Microsoft) and chip supply concentrated in Taiwan (pp. 33, 73).

One More Thing: The S-1 Warns About Its Own Readers

In May I joked that SpaceX illustrated its risk factors with a photo of a rocket on fire. Anthropic’s equivalent is a sentence: models may behave differently when they know they are being evaluated.

I find that oddly reassuring as a disclosure, and slightly unnerving as a reader. Every analyst on Wall Street is about to evaluate ANT. I hope it behaves.

Is it a good investment? That depends on the price, which isn’t in the document yet. What the document does show is a business whose unit economics turned positive this year, whose costs are locked in for a decade, and whose voting control is designed so that you, the shareholder, do not get the final say. You are buying the cash flows of a mission-driven company. The mission keeps the steering wheel.

All financial figures, contract terms, and quotations come from Anthropic, PBC’s preliminary Form S-1, filed with the SEC on October 26, 2026; page numbers refer to that document. All charts are my own, drawn from figures in the filing. The implied gross margin, compute per revenue dollar, and napkin valuation are my calculations, not figures reported by the company. The preliminary filing leaves the price range, deal size, and several metrics blank, so details may change in later amendments. This post is commentary, not investment advice.

item.title: FIFA Discovered the Commercial Break
item.dc:creator: He Ren
item.description:
American sports fans have spent their whole lives being trained to expect a break. The NFL has the two-minute warning and roughly a hundred stoppages. The NBA has quarters, timeouts, and a coach’s challenge that exists mostly so the network can sell you a truck. Soccer, famously, has none of this. Ninety minutes, two halves, one clock that never stops and never lies. You cannot cut to a car commercial mid-move, because there is no mid-move — the ball is always live.

This has always been a small tragedy for the people who sell advertising.

At the 2026 World Cup, that tragedy quietly ended. FIFA introduced a mandatory three-minute hydration break in each half of every match — around the 22nd minute and again around the 67th — regardless of the weather (FIFA). The stated reason is player welfare, and in the summer heat of Kansas City and Dallas, that reason is real. But if you squint at the timing, the structure, and the money, something else comes into focus: FIFA just gave the world’s most-watched sport its first built-in commercial break — and handed broadcasters a new pile of inventory to sell.

Let me walk through where FIFA’s money actually comes from, why television is the tail that wags the entire dog, and how a water break becomes a billion-dollar idea.

Where FIFA’s Money Actually Comes From

First, a myth to dispose of: FIFA does not primarily make its money from ticket sales, or from that overpriced beer at the stadium, or from selling jerseys. FIFA makes its money from selling the right to broadcast the World Cup, and secondarily from selling the right to associate your brand with the World Cup. Everything else is a rounding error by comparison.

Here is the budgeted revenue for the 2023–2026 cycle, which is how FIFA keeps its books (it thinks in four-year chunks anchored on a World Cup, not calendar years):

FIFA budgeted $11.0B for the 2023–26 cycle and has since revised its internal target upward toward ~$13B. Source: FIFA Annual Report 2022.
Revenue source 2023–26 budget Share
TV broadcasting rights $4.26B 39%
Hospitality & ticketing $3.10B 28%
Marketing (sponsorship) $2.69B 24%
Licensing rights $0.67B 6%
Other $0.28B 3%
Total $11.00B 100%

Two lines do almost two-thirds of the work: television and sponsorship. And these two are not independent — they are joined at the hip. A sponsor pays FIFA to put its logo where a billion people will see it, and the reason a billion people see it is television. Broadcasters pay for the audience; sponsors pay for access to that same audience. TV is the product, and everything else is priced off it.

Which is why the most important number on FIFA’s income statement is the one at the top — and why FIFA spends so much energy making that number bigger.

The Number That Never Stops Climbing

FIFA’s broadcasting revenue has gone up every single cycle, through scandal, through a pandemic, through a widely disliked Qatar tournament played in November. It is one of the most reliable upward-sloping lines in global media.

The 2026 tournament turbocharges this for reasons that have nothing to do with hydration:

  • It’s bigger. The field expanded from 32 teams to 48, and the match count ballooned from 64 to 104. More matches means more broadcast hours means more inventory to sell.
  • It’s in the right time zones. After Qatar’s inconvenient kickoffs, the 2026 tournament is hosted across the United States, Canada, and Mexico — meaning matches land in North American prime time and afternoon slots, the most valuable advertising windows on Earth.
  • The rights got more expensive. Industry estimates put the value of the 2026 TV rights 20–30% above Qatar 2022 (Rio Times). Fox reportedly paid $400–500 million for the English-language U.S. package alone.

Now hold that Fox number — $400–500 million for the whole tournament — in your head. We are about to compare it to something absurd.

The Other Half: Renting Out the Logo

If television is FIFA selling the audience, sponsorship is FIFA selling access to that audience — and it is sold, appropriately, as a pyramid. The higher you climb, the more exclusive the air and the thinner your wallet gets afterward.

FIFA’s three-tier sponsorship structure. FIFA does not publish per-brand fees; figures are industry estimates. Sources: Forbes; Zappi.
Tier What you get Est. price Examples (2026)
FIFA Partners Year-round rights across every FIFA competition; top billing ~$150–200M adidas, Coca-Cola, Visa, Hyundai-Kia, Lenovo, Qatar Airways, Aramco
World Cup Sponsors Rights to this tournament, worldwide ~$65–95M Budweiser, McDonald’s, Bank of America, Lay’s, Verizon, Unilever
Regional Supporters Rights within one region only ~$10–25M Regional brands across North America

The economics of the pyramid are ruthless and clever. There are only seven FIFA Partner slots, and that scarcity is the entire point — an adidas or a Visa is not really paying for a logo on a billboard, it is paying to keep a competitor off it. When Nike cannot be a FIFA Partner because adidas already is, the price adidas will pay to hold that exclusivity goes up. FIFA has monetized not just the space on the field but the absence of your rival from it.

And the pyramid, too, is ultimately priced off television. A World Cup Sponsor is buying pitchside LED boards, digital overlays, and the implied blessing of the tournament — all of which are worth precisely as much as the number of eyeballs the broadcast delivers. FIFA confirmed in March 2026 that all sixteen of its global sponsorship packages had sold out (Forbes), and total brand spending around the tournament — sponsorship plus the advertising that rides on it — is estimated north of $10 billion.

So both of FIFA’s big revenue lines, television and sponsorship, are really the same bet placed twice: how many people are watching, for how long, with how much attention? Anything that increases watching-time, or creates a fresh, attention-grabbing moment to sell, makes both lines go up at once.

Which is a very useful lens for thinking about a brand-new, perfectly-timed, guaranteed three-minute pause in the action.

Enter the Water Break

Here is the mechanical genius of the hydration break, from a television executive’s point of view.

Before 2026, cooling breaks existed, but only as an emergency measure. They were introduced at the 2014 World Cup in Brazil and could be called only when a heat index (WBGT) crossed a defined threshold (Kestrel Instruments). They were unpredictable. You could not sell an advertiser a slot that might or might not exist depending on the humidity in Rotterdam. Unpredictable inventory is nearly worthless inventory.

The 2026 rule changes exactly one thing, and it is the thing that matters: the breaks are now mandatory in every match, at a roughly fixed time, regardless of weather (Fox News / OutKick). Suddenly the inventory is guaranteed. An ad buyer can be promised a national commercial pod around minute 22 and minute 67 of a match watched by tens of millions of people, and the buyer can budget for it a year in advance. That is the difference between a puddle and a pipeline.

And notice what the schedule does to the shape of the game. A break at ~22 minutes and ~67 minutes carves each half neatly in two, turning a game of two 45-minute halves into something much more familiar to an American audience:

Old soccer New (2026)
Structure Two 45-min halves Four ~22-min “quarters”
Guaranteed stoppages Halftime only Halftime + 2 hydration breaks
Weather condition Cooling break only if hot Break every match, always
Sellable in-game ad pods 0 2 per match × 104 matches

France manager Didier Deschamps said it out loud: “It’s not two halftimes, it’s four quarter times… the players and the coaches adapt to this new reality” (ESPN). He meant it tactically. But “four quarters” is also, conveniently, the exact structure of the NBA and NFL broadcasts that American advertisers have optimized around for fifty years.

The Billion-Dollar Puddle

So what is a guaranteed in-game ad pod at the World Cup actually worth? The honest answer is that nobody knows precisely, because this is the first tournament with the inventory and FIFA and the broadcasters aren’t publishing the receipts. But the published estimates are eye-watering, and they cluster in a consistent range.

Analysts peg a single 30-second spot during a hydration break at $200,000 to $750,000, depending on the teams and the stage of the tournament, which works out to roughly $2.5 million to $9 million per match in fresh ad time across the two breaks (The Hollywood Reporter). Multiply across 104 matches and the estimates for Fox alone land at “at least $250 million, plausibly $500–600 million” (The Hollywood Reporter). Some global estimates, summing every broadcast market, run past $1 billion (Rio Times).

Here is the punchline in one chart:

Read that again. Fox paid roughly $400–500 million for the rights to broadcast the entire tournament. The advertising revenue from the hydration breaks alone — three minutes, twice a match — is estimated to plausibly reach $500–600 million. The garnish may be worth more than the meal.

And this compounds in FIFA’s favor on the next turn of the wheel. Broadcasters bid for rights based on how much money they can make from those rights. If the hydration break just made Fox’s package meaningfully more profitable, then the next rights auction starts from a higher floor. FIFA doesn’t even have to sell the ads itself — it simply raises the rent on the broadcasters who do. The water break pays FIFA twice: once by making the current tournament more valuable to Fox, and again by making the next set of rights more expensive.

To Be Fair to the Water

It would be too cynical — even for me — to claim this is only about money. Two things are true at once.

The player-welfare case is genuine. The 2026 tournament is being played in brutal conditions; matches in Kansas City, Dallas, and Monterrey have kicked off in temperatures well into the 90s Fahrenheit, and the 2025 Club World Cup (a dry run for all of this) featured genuinely dangerous heat. Giving players a structured chance to rehydrate is defensible sports science, and FIFA frames it exactly that way (FIFA).

But the criticism is also genuine, and it comes from two directions:

  • The scientists say three minutes is too short to meaningfully cool a body running at full exertion in extreme heat — useful, but more gesture than remedy when it’s truly sweltering (ESPN).
  • The coaches say the breaks distort the game. USWNT coach Emma Hayes calls them “momentum breaks” — a free tactical reset handed to whichever team is being outplayed (ESPN). Early tournament data hints she has a point: a striking share of goals arrived shortly after a break, when one side had just been allowed to regroup and re-instruct.

Notice that the strongest argument for the breaks (heat safety) would justify the old rule — call a break when it’s hot. It does not obviously justify the new rule — call a break in every match, including a temperate evening in Vancouver. The delta between “break when it’s hot” and “break always” is precisely the part that isn’t about hydration. That delta is the part you can sell.

The Tell

If you want to know what a rule is really for, watch who opts out.

The purest evidence that the hydration break is now an advertising vehicle is that some broadcasters are treating it as one — and a few are conspicuously refusing. In the U.S., Spanish-language broadcaster Telemundo declined to cut to commercials during the breaks, staying with studio analysis instead; U.K. broadcaster ITV did the same (ESPN). You do not have to make a principled decision about whether to run ads during a genuine medical timeout. You only face that decision if the “medical timeout” has quietly become the most valuable ninety seconds of unsold airtime in the building.

FIFA has spent a decade proving that its revenue line only points one way, and it has done it by relentlessly finding new surfaces to sell. It expanded the field to 48 teams. It moved the tournament into American prime time. It launched a 32-team Club World Cup out of thin air. The hydration break is the same instinct applied to the one piece of the product that had always resisted it: the ninety uninterrupted minutes themselves.

So drink up. Somewhere, an accountant is very, very hydrated.

Revenue figures are from FIFA’s own budget and financial statements, linked inline. Advertising figures for the hydration breaks are analyst and press estimates, not official FIFA or broadcaster disclosures, and should be read as such. All charts are the author’s own, built from the cited data. No copyrighted imagery is used.

item.title: SpaceX Filed an S-1. It Reads Like a Magazine.
item.dc:creator: He Ren
item.description:
Normally, when a company files for an IPO, the document looks like a tax form. Times New Roman. Gray boxes. 280 pages of legalese designed to make your eyes glaze over before page 12.

SpaceX’s S-1, filed May 20, 2026, is not that.

Within the first few pages is a full-bleed photograph of Mars. From there on, the document is sprinkled with dozens more embedded images — full-bleed launch photos, Elon pull-quote posters, glossy product spec sheets for every rocket in the fleet, and a “RISK FACTORS” section opener that is, no exaggeration, a photograph of a rocket on fire. (We’ll get to that one.)

The whole thing reads more like a coffee-table magazine than an SEC filing. Which sets the tone — and signals the next several billion dollars they want from you. Let’s walk through it.

What Was Filed

The company is Space Exploration Technologies Corp., headquartered at 1 Rocket Road, Starbase, Texas. (Yes, “Starbase” is now an actual incorporated town. No, I am not making that up.)

The ticker will be SPCX, dual-listed on Nasdaq and the brand-new Nasdaq Texas exchange — because when your CEO is in Texas, your rockets launch from Texas, and your headquarters is in Texas, you may as well list on the Texas exchange too. Goldman Sachs is the lead bank, with Morgan Stanley, BofA, Citi, JPMorgan, and Barclays just behind. Then seventeen more banks pile in underneath, presumably for moral support.

The price isn’t in the document yet — they fill that in closer to the roadshow — but reporting around the filing puts it at roughly $1.75 trillion valuation, a ~$75 billion raise, and a June 12 listing, with an indicative price of $525–530 per share (TradingKey; NBC News).

For reference: $1.75T puts SpaceX between Amazon and Alphabet in market cap on day one. The IPO alone would make Musk a trillionaire on paper. No pressure.

The Company Is Now Three Businesses, Not One

The fact most people haven’t fully absorbed yet: SpaceX quietly absorbed xAI on February 2, 2026, in what the lawyers call a “transaction between entities under common control.” Translation: Musk owned both, so he merged them. The company you’re buying into is no longer just a rocket company. It’s a rocket company, an internet company, and an AI company, stapled together by the same controlling shareholder.

The three businesses make money in extremely different ways. One mints cash. One spends a fortune on the next rocket. One spends a fortune on, well, chips.

All figures FY 2025, in USD billions.
Segment Revenue Op result Capex
Space (Falcon, Dragon, Starship) 4.1 (0.7) 3.8
Connectivity (Starlink) 11.4 4.4 4.2
AI (xAI, Grok, X) 3.2 (6.4) 12.7
Total 18.7 (2.6) 20.7

Three quick takeaways:

  • Starlink is the engine. Revenue grew 50% year over year. Operating income grew 120%. It’s the only segment making real money, and it’s making a lot of it.
  • Space looks like a loser, but it isn’t really. Starship development swallowed $3 billion of 2025 spend. Strip that out and the launch business — Falcon 9, Falcon Heavy, Dragon — is comfortably profitable. The headline loss is because Musk is building the next rocket.
  • AI is the hungry one. $12.7 billion in capex in 2025, plus another $7.7 billion in Q1 2026 alone, against $3.2 billion of revenue. AI is the bet that lives downstream of Starlink’s cash flow.

In one sentence: you are buying a satellite internet company that happens to own a rocket factory and a giant warehouse full of GPUs.

Two Classes of Stock, One Person in Charge

The cap structure section is short, important, and a little spicy.

After the IPO, there will be two classes of stock:

  • Class A — what you buy on the open market. One vote per share.
  • Class B — held by Musk. Ten votes per share. And the kicker: Class B holders, voting as a class, elect a majority of the board on their own.

The S-1 spells it out plainly. Musk will control the outcome of anything that requires a shareholder vote, and SpaceX will use the “controlled company” exemption from a bunch of Nasdaq governance rules — including the one that usually requires a majority of independent directors on the board.

If you’ve followed Google, Meta, or Snap IPOs, you’ve seen this movie. Founder-controlled tech companies do it all the time. What’s a little different here is that Musk doesn’t even need to win a Class A vote. Class B alone elects a majority of the board. You’re buying the cash flows. Musk keeps the steering wheel.

For passive investors, this matters in one specific way: index providers have been getting increasingly grumpy about super-voting structures, and the prospectus itself lists “exclusion from certain stock indices” as a risk factor. Even at $1.75 trillion, S&P 500 admission on day one is not guaranteed.

The $1.25 Billion-a-Month Anthropic Contract

Now we get to the section that made me re-read the filing to make sure I wasn’t hallucinating.

On May 3, 2026, SpaceX (using the data centers it inherited from xAI) signed a Cloud Services Agreement with Anthropic — the AI lab founded by former OpenAI researchers, makers of Claude. The terms:

Pursuant to these agreements, the customer has agreed to pay us $1.25 billion per month through May 2029.

That’s $15 billion a year. For three years. From Anthropic. To Elon Musk’s company.

Let’s appreciate this for a second. Anthropic was founded by people who left OpenAI. OpenAI was co-founded by Elon Musk before he stormed out and started xAI. Now Anthropic is renting GPUs from Musk’s xAI to train Claude, the model that competes most directly with ChatGPT.

It’s the corporate equivalent of buying batteries from your ex.

The strategy actually makes sense for both sides, despite the optics:

  • Anthropic has more money than it can spend on chips. They just raised $30B at a $380B valuation (Forge). What they don’t have is electricity. xAI’s Memphis data centers came online in 122 days flat — a terrestrial speedrun — and have capacity to spare. Anthropic rents what they need.
  • xAI/SpaceX gets to fund its own AI lab by selling compute to its biggest model competitor. This is exactly what OpenAI did to Microsoft in 2019. Except now SpaceX is playing the Microsoft role.

The optics are funny. The strategic logic is solid.

The $60 Billion Option on Cursor

The Anthropic deal is the big one. The Cursor deal is the weird one.

In April 2026, SpaceX signed a “compute and option agreement” with Cursor — yes, that Cursor, the AI-powered code editor that every software engineer you know is currently using. The terms:

  • SpaceX gives Cursor GPU capacity to run their product.
  • SpaceX has the option to buy Cursor at an implied equity value of $60 billion, payable in SPCX stock.
  • If SpaceX walks away, they owe Cursor $10 billion in pre-baked break-up fees ($1.5B option termination + $8.5B deferred compute services).

Why would a rocket company want to buy a code editor? The S-1 is fairly honest about it. Cursor’s millions of developers generate “context-rich, verifiable data” about how humans actually write code — exactly the kind of training fuel that improves an AI model. You’re not buying a code editor. You’re buying a giant pipeline of human coding behavior, which happens to come wrapped inside a code editor.

This structure is genuinely new. It’s the same compute-today-equity-tomorrow dance Microsoft did with OpenAI and Amazon did with Anthropic, but now applied one layer higher — at the application layer instead of the model layer. If it works, expect to see more of it. The next twelve months will probably involve a lot of AI startups being offered “free” compute that comes with a $40 billion option attached.

OpenAI: The Two-Sentence Mention That Should Have Been Much Longer

The full S-1 mentions OpenAI exactly twice, both in routine “we have competitors” boilerplate. There is no mention of the lawsuit Musk filed in 2024 trying to block OpenAI’s for-profit conversion and force out Sam Altman.

Why? Because two days before this S-1 was filed, a federal jury in California threw the lawsuit out.

The verdict landed on May 18, 2026. The jurors deliberated for less than two hours (NPR; Axios; NBC News). They didn’t even rule on the merits — they decided Musk had simply waited too long to sue. Statute of limitations. Game over. Musk’s related claim against Microsoft was dismissed on the same grounds.

Musk’s lawyer told reporters: “This one is not over. I can sum it up in one word: appeal.” Sure.

But the timing is impossible to ignore. Filing a $75 billion IPO the same week your big-ticket lawsuit against your biggest AI rival gets dismissed in two hours is — let’s say — convenient. The cloud that would have hung over SPCX’s risk factors evaporated three trading days before the prospectus went public.

And in case you thought OpenAI was just going to sit there and watch Musk go public alone: on the same day this prospectus dropped, multiple outlets reported that OpenAI is preparing to confidentially file its own S-1, with the same lead banks (Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley), targeting a fall debut at a valuation that “exceeds $1 trillion” (Bloomberg; Axios; CNBC).

So: in one week, Musk’s lawsuit against OpenAI dies, SpaceX files publicly, and OpenAI files confidentially. None of that is quite planets-aligning, but it’s close.

Three Giants in Twelve Months

Three of the largest IPOs in the history of public markets are about to hit within roughly one calendar year:

Company Filing status Target listing Indicative size / valuation Lead banks
SpaceX S-1 public, May 20, 2026 June 12, 2026 ~$75B raise / ~$1.75T Goldman, Morgan Stanley
OpenAI Confidential S-1 imminent Fall 2026 (~September) >$1T valuation Goldman, Morgan Stanley
Anthropic Not filed; ~Q4 2026 expected More likely 2027 ~$60B+ raise / $380B+ Not announced

A few notes:

The same two banks are running two of these deals. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are leading both SpaceX and OpenAI. For deals this big and this competitively sensitive, that’s unusual — normally the banks would split clients. The same teams will pitch Musk’s company in June and Altman’s company in September. The “Chinese walls” inside investment banks (the rules that supposedly stop one client’s confidential info from leaking to another) are about to get a real-world stress test.

The flow event is going to be loud. SPCX at $1.75T would be a top-10 weight in any major US index that admits it. If OpenAI joins in the fall at $1T+, you’d have two of the five biggest companies in the world IPO’ing within five months. Every S&P 500 fund and Nasdaq-100 fund on Earth would need to buy a lot of stock, all on the same admission day. Quant desks have been modeling this for a quarter.

Anthropic gets to wait. They have $30B of run-rate revenue, just raised $30B, and have the cleanest equity story of the three — no founder-control questions, no rival lawsuits, no for-profit-conversion drama. Their stated plan is a 2027 listing. Filing third may turn out to be the best slot of the three.

One More Thing: Possibly the First S-1 With Posters

Which brings us back to the cover.

A typical S-1 has exactly one image: the company logo, on page one. The ratio of text to pictures is roughly that of the IRS Form 1040 instructions.

SpaceX’s S-1 has dozens of embedded images. Among them:

  • A full-bleed photograph of Mars from orbit.
  • Multiple full-page Musk pull-quotes set against glamour shots of Starship in flight.
  • A “SPACE — ACTIVATED 2002 — FIRSTS” infographic with launch counts, reused-booster percentages, and crewmembers flown.
  • A photograph of Starman (the spacesuit mannequin SpaceX launched on a Tesla Roadster in 2018, currently floating somewhere between Mars and the asteroid belt).
  • Glossy spec sheets for Falcon 9, Falcon Heavy, Dragon, Starship, and Starlink V3.
  • A “RISK FACTORS” section opener that is, literally, a photograph of a rocket surrounded by fire.

That last one is not metaphorical:

The page where the company discusses what could go horribly wrong with the business is, in the prospectus itself, illustrated by an image of their main product on fire.

Coinbase, Airbnb, and Roblox were the previous gold-standard for “S-1 with design sense” — branded color blocks, full-bleed photos, the occasional pull quote. None of them put a photograph of their core product on actual fire as the masthead of their risk factors. SpaceX may be the first.

There’s a real argument that this is part of the offering. When you’re trying to convince public-market investors to buy into a controlled company with an AI segment burning $12B a year and a CEO with a non-zero probability of any given Tuesday being interesting, “trust us, the vibes are great” is a legitimate strategy. The prospectus isn’t selling a document. It’s selling a feeling.

It’s also, in fairness, the only S-1 you can read twice without falling asleep. That might be worth a few basis points all by itself.

Financial figures and contract terms come from Space Exploration Technologies Corp.’s Form S-1, filed with the SEC on May 20, 2026. Images shown are downsampled reproductions of figures in the same filing. External reporting cited inline.

item.title: Time Value of Money on the BA II Plus and in Excel
item.dc:creator: He Ren
item.description:
Why Two Tools?

Most introductory finance problems can be cracked two ways: on a TI BA II Plus financial calculator or in a spreadsheet. The calculator is what you bring to an exam; Excel is what you use at work. They give the same answer, but the workflow is different — the calculator stores one problem in memory, while Excel makes inputs visible and easy to tweak.

This post is a practical walkthrough for an undergraduate finance student. We start with calculator setup, move through the core TVM problems, and finish with NPV and IRR for uneven cash flows. Every example shows both the calculator keystrokes and the Excel formula.

Setting Up the BA II Plus

Out of the box, the BA II Plus has two defaults that trip up students. Fix them once.

1. Set decimal places to 4 (or more). Press 2nd → FORMAT → enter 4 → ENTER → 2nd → QUIT.

2. Set payments per year to 1. Press 2nd → P/Y → enter 1 → ENTER → 2nd → QUIT. This is the safer default. When you have monthly compounding, you can either change P/Y to 12 or leave P/Y at 1 and enter the periodic rate manually (e.g., 0.5 for 6% / 12). I recommend the second approach — fewer hidden settings to forget.

3. Confirm END mode (not BGN). Most problems use end-of-period cash flows. Press 2nd → BGN. If it says END, press 2nd → QUIT. If it says BGN, press 2nd → SET → 2nd → QUIT.

4. Clear the TVM registers before every new problem. Press 2nd → CLR TVM. The calculator remembers your last problem; failing to clear is the #1 source of wrong answers on exams.

Sign convention

The BA II Plus uses cash flow signs. Money you pay out is negative; money you receive is positive. If PV and FV have the same sign, the calculator returns an error. This convention matches Excel.

The Five TVM Keys

Every basic time value problem uses some subset of five variables, four of which you know and one you solve for.

Key Meaning Excel argument
N Number of periods nper
I/Y Interest rate per period (as a percent) rate
PV Present value (lump sum today) pv
PMT Recurring payment each period pmt
FV Future value (lump sum at the end) fv

One pitfall: in the BA II Plus, you enter I/Y as a percent (5 means 5%), but Excel’s rate argument wants a decimal (0.05). Forgetting this is the #2 source of wrong answers.

The next four examples walk through solving for each of the lump-sum unknowns — FV, PV, N, and I/Y — one at a time.

Example 1 — Solving for FV (future value of a lump sum)

You deposit $1,000 today in an account earning 5% per year. What is the balance in 10 years?

BA II Plus:

Step Keystrokes Display
1 2nd CLR TVM 0
2 10 N N = 10
3 5 I/Y I/Y = 5
4 1000 +/− PV PV = −1,000
5 0 PMT PMT = 0
6 CPT FV FV = 1,628.89

Excel: =FV(0.05, 10, 0, -1000) → 1,628.89

Example 2 — Solving for PV (present value of a lump sum)

You’d like to have $50,000 saved for a down payment in 5 years. Your savings earn 6% per year. How much do you need to deposit today?

BA II Plus:

Step Keystrokes Display
1 2nd CLR TVM 0
2 5 N N = 5
3 6 I/Y I/Y = 6
4 0 PMT PMT = 0
5 50000 FV FV = 50,000
6 CPT PV PV = −37,362.91

The negative sign means it’s an outflow today — you pay $37,362.91 now to receive $50,000 in five years.

Excel: =PV(0.06, 5, 0, 50000) → −37,362.91

Example 3 — Solving for N (how long?)

You invest $5,000 today at 8% per year. How many years until it doubles to $10,000?

BA II Plus:

Step Keystrokes Display
1 2nd CLR TVM 0
2 8 I/Y I/Y = 8
3 5000 +/− PV PV = −5,000
4 0 PMT PMT = 0
5 10000 FV FV = 10,000
6 CPT N N = 9.0065

So it takes a little over nine years. (This is a quick check on the “Rule of 72”: 72 / 8 = 9 years, which is close.)

Excel: =NPER(0.08, 0, -5000, 10000) → 9.0065

Example 4 — Solving for I/Y (what rate did I earn?)

A friend tells you they bought a stock for $1,000 six years ago and just sold it for $1,500. What annualized rate of return did they earn?

BA II Plus:

Step Keystrokes Display
1 2nd CLR TVM 0
2 6 N N = 6
3 1000 +/− PV PV = −1,000
4 0 PMT PMT = 0
5 1500 FV FV = 1,500
6 CPT I/Y I/Y = 6.9913

Roughly 6.99% per year.

Excel: =RATE(6, 0, -1000, 1500) → 0.069913

Example 5 — Future value of an annuity (monthly contributions)

Now add PMT to the mix.

You save $300 at the end of every month for 30 years in an account earning 7% APR compounded monthly. What’s the balance at the end?

The trick: convert annual quantities to monthly before you enter them. Periodic rate = 7% / 12 ≈ 0.5833%. Number of periods = 30 × 12 = 360.

BA II Plus:

Step Keystrokes Display
1 2nd CLR TVM 0
2 360 N N = 360
3 7 ÷ 12 = I/Y I/Y = 0.5833
4 0 PV PV = 0
5 300 +/− PMT PMT = −300
6 CPT FV FV = 365,990.62

Excel: =FV(0.07/12, 360, -300, 0) → 365,990.62

APR vs EAR

The annual percentage rate (APR) is the stated, nominal rate. The effective annual rate (EAR) is what you actually earn or pay once compounding is accounted for. For any compounding frequency above 1, EAR > APR.

Example 6 — Converting APR to EAR

A credit card charges 18% APR compounded monthly. What’s the EAR?

BA II Plus: the ICONV worksheet does this in three keystrokes.

Step Keystrokes Display
1 2nd ICONV NOM =
2 18 ENTER ↓ C/Y =
3 12 ENTER ↑ CPT EFF = 19.5618

Excel: =EFFECT(0.18, 12) → 0.195618

Going the other way — from EAR to APR — use NOMINAL: =NOMINAL(0.195618, 12) → 0.18

Mortgages

A mortgage is just a present-value annuity problem in disguise. The bank lends you the present value; you repay with level monthly payments that include both principal and interest.

Example 7 — Monthly payment

You borrow $400,000 on a 30-year mortgage at 6.5% APR (compounded monthly). What’s the monthly payment?

BA II Plus:

Step Keystrokes Display
1 2nd CLR TVM 0
2 360 N N = 360
3 6.5 ÷ 12 = I/Y I/Y = 0.5417
4 400000 PV PV = 400,000
5 0 FV FV = 0
6 CPT PMT PMT = −2,528.27

The negative sign means you’re paying out each month.

Excel: =PMT(0.065/12, 360, 400000) → −2,528.27

Each monthly payment is split between interest (charged on the outstanding balance) and principal (which reduces that balance). Early on, the balance is huge, so almost all of the payment is interest. Late in the loan, the balance is small, and most of the payment goes to principal. Excel exposes this split directly: IPMT returns the interest portion of a given payment and PPMT returns the principal portion. For month 1 of this loan:

  • =IPMT(0.065/12, 1, 360, 400000) → −2,166.67
  • =PPMT(0.065/12, 1, 360, 400000) → −361.60

Together they sum to the full payment. By month 360, the proportions are reversed.

Uneven Cash Flows: NPV

When the cash flows aren’t level, the basic TVM keys aren’t enough — you discount each cash flow on its own and add them up. On the BA II Plus, this is the CF (cash flow) worksheet.

Example 8 — NPV of a project

A project costs $10,000 today. It pays $2,000 at the end of year 1, $3,000 in year 2, $4,000 in year 3, and $5,000 in year 4. The discount rate is 10%. What’s the NPV?

BA II Plus: the CF worksheet stores cash flows by period.

Step Keystrokes Display
1 CF 2nd CLR WORK CF0 = 0
2 10000 +/− ENTER ↓ CF0 = −10,000
3 2000 ENTER ↓ ↓ C01 = 2,000
4 3000 ENTER ↓ ↓ C02 = 3,000
5 4000 ENTER ↓ ↓ C03 = 4,000
6 5000 ENTER ↓ ↓ C04 = 5,000
7 NPV 10 ENTER ↓ CPT NPV = 717.85

The ↓ ↓ between cash flows skips past the “frequency” prompt (F01, F02, …). If you have the same cash flow repeated several years in a row, you can enter the value once and set the frequency instead of typing it multiple times.

Excel: Excel’s NPV function discounts the first cash flow back one period, so you have to add the time-zero outflow separately.

=NPV(0.10, 2000, 3000, 4000, 5000) - 10000 → 717.85

The =NPV gotcha

Excel’s NPV assumes the first argument is one period away. The time-zero cash flow goes outside the function. Many wrong answers come from including -10000 inside the NPV parentheses.

IRR

The internal rate of return is the discount rate that makes NPV exactly zero. It’s the project’s break-even rate.

Example 9 — IRR of the same project

BA II Plus: with the cash flows from Example 8 still loaded, just press:

IRR CPT → IRR = 12.8258

Excel: put the cash flows in a column (including the −10,000 at time zero) and call:

=IRR(A1:A5) → 0.128258

Because the IRR (12.83%) is greater than the 10% discount rate used in Example 8, the project’s NPV is positive — exactly what we found. In general, accept a project when IRR > the required rate of return.

When IRR misleads

IRR can have multiple solutions when cash flows change sign more than once (e.g., −, +, +, −). For mutually exclusive projects, IRR can also rank projects differently than NPV. NPV is the safer decision rule; IRR is the more intuitive one to communicate.

Cheat Sheet

Task BA II Plus Excel
Future value of lump sum N I/Y PV 0 PMT CPT FV =FV(rate, nper, 0, -pv)
Present value of lump sum N I/Y FV 0 PMT CPT PV =PV(rate, nper, 0, -fv)
Number of periods I/Y PV PMT FV CPT N =NPER(rate, pmt, pv, fv)
Periodic rate N PV PMT FV CPT I/Y =RATE(nper, pmt, pv, fv)
Annuity payment N I/Y PV FV CPT PMT =PMT(rate, nper, pv, fv)
APR → EAR 2nd ICONV, enter NOM and C/Y, CPT EFF =EFFECT(apr, m)
EAR → APR 2nd ICONV, enter EFF and C/Y, CPT NOM =NOMINAL(ear, m)
NPV (uneven cash flows) CF worksheet, then NPV rate ENTER ↓ CPT =NPV(rate, cf1:cfn) + cf0
IRR CF worksheet, then IRR CPT =IRR(cf0:cfn)
Interest portion of payment (Calculate manually from balance × rate) =IPMT(rate, period, nper, pv)
Principal portion of payment (Payment minus interest portion) =PPMT(rate, period, nper, pv)

Closing Thoughts

Three habits will save you in this class:

  1. Always clear the calculator (2nd CLR TVM for TVM keys, 2nd CLR WORK inside CF) before starting a new problem.
  2. Match the period. If the problem is monthly, your N, I/Y, and PMT all need to be monthly. Mixing annual and monthly is the most common error.
  3. Watch the signs. If you put money in (a loan, an investment), it’s negative. If you take money out (a withdrawal, a repayment), it’s positive. Excel and the BA II Plus follow the same rule.

When you graduate, you’ll do almost everything in Excel — once a problem is bigger than the five TVM keys, the spreadsheet wins. But knowing both makes you faster, and it gives you a sanity check: if the calculator and the spreadsheet disagree, you’ve made a setup mistake somewhere, and you’ll catch it before turning it in.

item.title: Summary: From EDGAR Filings to a Structured Database
item.dc:creator: He Ren
item.description:
Overview

A summary of Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham’s article.

This follow-up to the earlier HMDA post walks through a complete, end-to-end research pipeline built with Claude Code: pulling 10-K filings from SEC EDGAR, parsing out the Risk Factors section, and loading the results into a queryable database. The motivating research question is whether trade-exposed U.S. firms ramped up tariff-related language in their risk disclosures after the 2025 tariff escalation. The broader methodological point is that a researcher can go from a raw internet source to an analyzable dataset in roughly half an hour.

The Pipeline

The author builds the pipeline in phases, with Claude Code first entering “plan mode” to read EDGAR API documentation and propose an approach before writing any code. The phases:

  1. Research and planning. Claude reads EDGAR docs and proposes a design.
  2. Design clarification. Claude asks the researcher to choose between DuckDB and SQLite, between simple keyword search and LLM classification, and what User-Agent string to use.
  3. CIK lookup. Claude resolves Central Index Keys for 29 of 30 target firms. Gap Inc. fails because its ticker had changed (GPS → GAP).
  4. Filing index queries. Claude hits the EDGAR API for each firm’s 10-Ks from 2022 to 2025.
  5. Download. Raw HTML filings are downloaded with caching so reruns avoid redundant network calls.
  6. Parsing. BeautifulSoup extracts Item 1A (Risk Factors), with regex tweaks for filings that split “Item 1A” and “Risk Factors” across lines.
  7. Storage. Parsed text is loaded into DuckDB, alongside tariff keyword counts and context snippets.
  8. Quality reports. An extraction-quality report flags parsing failures, which is how the author catches the Honeywell and Intel regex issue.
  9. Querying. SQL queries against DuckDB produce the descriptive results.

The final dataset covers 119 of 120 filings successfully parsed. Total code: roughly 480 lines of Python.

The Original Prompts

Initial prompt

I want to build a dataset of 10-K Risk Factors from SEC EDGAR to study how tariff-related risk disclosure changed 2022–2025. Here’s what I know about EDGAR:

  • Every company has a CIK (Central Index Key)
  • The EDGAR filing API is at https://efts.sec.gov/LATEST/
  • Rate limit: 10 requests/second, must include User-Agent header

I want 10-Ks for ~30 trade-exposed firms — manufacturing, retail, tech hardware. Caterpillar, Nike, Apple, Deere, Ford, 3M, Intel…

Execution

Run it for the full list. Let’s see how it goes.

Querying the database

Which firms mentioned tariffs the most?

Key Findings

The descriptive results aren’t the main point, but they validate the pipeline:

  • John Deere had the highest tariff mention count, rising from three to four mentions over the period.
  • The 2022–2025 sample produced 26–35 tariff-related paragraphs per year, compared to 25 total across 18 firms in a 2010 baseline.
  • Language shifted from generic phrases like “changes in trade policy” to specific references — Section 301, particular product categories, “liberation day.”
  • Walmart did not mention tariffs until its 2025 filing.
  • Retail firms mentioned tariffs less often than manufacturing or tech-hardware firms.

Lessons

Front-load the scraping context. Specifying rate limits, headers, and API structure up front saves debugging rounds later.

Let Claude ask design questions. Instead of pre-specifying every detail, give Claude the high-level task and let it surface design choices (DuckDB vs. SQLite, keyword search vs. classification). The researcher’s job is to make the calls.

Build resume capability in. Network failures are common. Caching and idempotent scripts make reruns cheap — the Gap Inc. ticker fix required only four new downloads in 43 seconds, not a full re-pull.

Generate extraction-quality reports. They are how subtle parsing bugs get caught before they corrupt months of downstream analysis.

SQL beats CSVs for text-as-data. DuckDB gives zero-config deployment, SQL queryability, and relational structure without running a server.

Conclusion

The pipeline is small — one researcher, one afternoon, 480 lines of Python — but it shows how the per-project cost of building real research infrastructure has dropped. The interesting question is no longer whether the pipeline is feasible, but which research questions are worth pointing it at.

item.title: Summary: Large Datasets and Structured Databases
item.dc:creator: He Ren
item.description:
Overview

A summary of Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham’s article, published April 5, 2026.

Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham argues that AI coding agents (specifically Claude Code) have collapsed the fixed costs of professional data engineering, making it feasible for economists to build harmonized, documented, queryable databases from massive government datasets without specialized data engineering training.

The Core Problem

Economists traditionally work with flat CSV files and copies because learning proper data infrastructure (parquet files, databases, schemas) required significant upfront investment. This made messy workflows a rational choice — the fixed cost of “doing it right” was too high to justify for one-off projects.

The Demonstration

To prove the point, the author transformed a 70GB HMDA (Home Mortgage Disclosure Act) mortgage dataset — 291 million rows across 18 years — into a professional-grade pipeline using Claude Code. Work that traditionally takes weeks now takes hours.

Key results

  • Downloaded and harmonized 18 years of mortgage data from two incompatible sources (2007–2017 vs. 2018–2024)
  • Achieved 15× compression converting CSVs to parquet (70GB → 6GB)
  • Built a DuckDB database with a queryable metadata table documenting every column
  • Created county-by-year aggregate tables (HHI concentration, denial rates, median loan amounts, etc.)
  • Classified lenders as fintech vs. traditional banks
  • Found fintech origination share grew from ~1.1% (2007) to a peak of 16.3% (2021), settling around 11% by 2024

The Original Prompts

Initial comprehensive prompt

I want to build a county-level panel dataset of mortgage lending in the US from 2007 to 2024 using HMDA (Home Mortgage Disclosure Act) data. The goal is to study the geographic expansion of fintech mortgage lenders over time.

The data comes from two sources (I’ve verified both are accessible):

  • 2007–2017: CFPB historic data at https://files.consumerfinance.gov/hmda-historic-loan-data/hmda_{YEAR}_nationwide_all-records_codes.zip. These are zipped CSVs with numeric codes and the old LAR column names.
  • 2018–2024: CFPB Data Browser API at https://ffiec.cfpb.gov/v2/data-browser-api/view/nationwide/csv?years={YEAR}. These stream as CSV with 99 columns, string codes, and the new format (uses lei instead of respondent_id, different column names throughout).

Each year is millions of rows. The full panel is 250M+ rows. This will not fit in pandas.

Here’s what I’d like you to do:

  1. Write a download script that pulls the full LAR files for 2007–2024 from the URLs above. Include resume capability in case downloads get interrupted. Use a proper User-Agent header.
  2. Convert each year’s CSV to parquet for efficient storage.
  3. Set up a DuckDB database. Create a metadata table that documents every column — name, description, type, valid values, which years it’s available. This metadata table is important: I want future sessions to be able to query it and immediately understand the dataset without me re-explaining anything.

Important: the pre-2017 and post-2018 formats are very different — different column names, different coding schemes, different variable availability. You’ll need to figure out a crosswalk and harmonize into a consistent schema.

Key variables I care about: year, lender ID, lender name, county FIPS, state FIPS, loan type, loan purpose, action taken (originated, denied, etc.), loan amount, applicant race, applicant income. Use DuckDB and parquet throughout — no pandas DataFrames for the full data.

Feasibility inquiry

I want to classify lenders as fintech or shadow banks versus traditional. Start with the lender classification from Fuster, Plosser, Schnabl and Vickery (2019). Tell me what it would take to do this task before you try anything complicated. Is this feasible? What might be missing?

Aggregate table request

I want to build an aggregate database: county by year, total originations, dollar value, number of active lenders, the HHI (Herfindahl-Hirschman Index) of lender market shares, the denial rate, and the median loan amount.

Visualization request

Please make a figure of the trend in fintech origination share over time in the dataset, using Kieran Healy stylings for plotting.

Key Insights

Metadata as context engineering. The metadata table acts as a form of “context engineering for data” — it stores column descriptions, valid values, and availability information directly inside the database. Future sessions can query the documentation without the human having to re-explain.

Right tools for big data. When data exceeds RAM, parquet and DuckDB are the right tools — pandas is the wrong tool.

Plan before coding. For complex pipelines, asking the model to scope the task before implementation pays off (the feasibility prompt above is a good example).

Conclusion

The author argues that AI-assisted data engineering has fundamentally shifted the economics of research infrastructure. The bottleneck for empirical work has moved from “can I build the infrastructure?” to “do I have a worthwhile research question?”

Key takeaways:

  • The fixed costs of professional data engineering have collapsed
  • Large public datasets are more accessible than commonly assumed
  • Embedding metadata in the database makes future work cheaper
  • Planning matters more than coding speed
